title: Van't Hoff Factor and Colligative Property Formulas

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part I, Class 12 — Solutions

expression: ΔTf = i·Kf·m  ;  ΔTb = i·Kb·m  ;  π = i·CRT
explanation: Colligative properties depend only on the NUMBER of solute particles in solution, not their identity — freezing point depression, boiling point elevation, and osmotic pressure all include the van't Hoff factor i, which corrects for solutes that dissociate (i > 1, e.g. NaCl → i ≈ 2) or associate (i < 1, e.g. some carboxylic acids dimerising in non-polar solvents). For a non-electrolyte that neither dissociates nor associates, i = 1 exactly.

variables.meaning: Freezing point depression, boiling point elevation
Molal freezing point depression / boiling point elevation constants
Molar concentration, gas constant, absolute temperature

workedExample.scenario: A 0.1 molal NaCl solution (fully dissociates, i ≈ 2), Kf(water) = 1.86 K·kg/mol.
workedExample.result: ΔTf = 0.372 K (freezing point lowered by this much more than a non-electrolyte at the same molality)

commonMistakes: Forgetting the van't Hoff factor entirely for ionic solutes — this underestimates the actual colligative effect, since each formula unit produces multiple particles in solution.
Using molarity instead of molality in the freezing point depression/boiling point elevation formulas — these specifically require molality, since it doesn't change with temperature.
genZNote: Van't Hoff factor: it's not about what the solute IS, it's about how many particles it splits into.
